question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.103, a residential landlord must refund a tenant's security deposit within how many days after the tenant surrenders the premises (subject to the tenant furnishing a forwarding address)?
choice_a: 30 days
choice_b: 10 days
choice_c: 60 days
choice_d: 90 days
explanation: Property Code Section 92.103 requires a residential landlord to refund a security deposit not later than the 30th day after the tenant surrenders the premises, except as affected by the tenant's obligation under Section 92.107 to furnish a forwarding address.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.103 (obligation to refund), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.109(d), a residential landlord who fails to either refund the security deposit or provide a written, itemized list of deductions within 30 days after the tenant surrenders the premises is:
choice_a: Presumed to have acted in bad faith
choice_b: Automatically forgiven of any obligation to account for the deposit
choice_c: Entitled to keep the entire deposit without explanation
choice_d: Only liable if the tenant can prove the landlord's subjective intent to defraud
explanation: Property Code Section 92.109(d) creates a rebuttable presumption of bad faith when a landlord fails to timely return the deposit or provide the required itemized deductions within the 30-day window, shifting the practical burden onto the landlord to justify the retention.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.109(d) (presumption of bad faith), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.109(a), a residential landlord found to have acted in bad faith in retaining a security deposit is liable to the tenant for:
choice_a: $100 plus three times the portion of the deposit wrongfully withheld, plus the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees
choice_b: A flat $50 penalty regardless of the amount withheld
choice_c: Return of the deposit only, with no additional penalty
choice_d: Criminal restitution ordered by a municipal court
explanation: Property Code Section 92.109(a) sets a specific statutory bad-faith penalty formula -- $100 plus three times the amount of the deposit wrongfully withheld, plus the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees in a suit to recover the deposit -- a materially different remedy than merely repaying the withheld amount.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.109(a) (bad faith retention penalty formula), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.107, if a departing residential tenant never gives the landlord a forwarding address for purposes of a security deposit refund, the tenant:
choice_a: Does not forfeit the right to a deposit refund or itemized damages description merely for failing to provide a forwarding address, though the landlord is not obligated to act until an address is given
choice_b: Automatically forfeits the entire deposit
choice_c: Must sue within 10 days or lose all rights to the deposit
choice_d: Can never recover the deposit under any circumstances
explanation: Section 92.107 relieves the landlord of the duty to refund the deposit or provide an itemized damages list until the tenant furnishes a forwarding address, but expressly clarifies that a tenant's failure to provide one does not forfeit the underlying right to the refund or accounting.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.107 (forwarding address requirement), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.052, a residential landlord's duty to repair or remedy a condition materially affecting a tenant's physical health or safety is triggered only when the tenant gives notice to the landlord and:
choice_a: Is not delinquent in the payment of rent at the time notice is given
choice_b: Has lived in the unit for at least one full year
choice_c: Pays an additional repair deposit at the time of notice
choice_d: Obtains a court order compelling the repair
explanation: Property Code Section 92.052 conditions the landlord's duty to repair on the tenant giving notice (specifying the condition) to the person or place where rent is normally paid, and on the tenant not being delinquent in rent when that notice is given -- a frequently tested precondition to the repair remedies in Subchapter B.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.052(a) (landlord's duty to repair -- rent-current precondition), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.056, once a tenant has given proper notice of a condition requiring repair, how many days is presumed to be a 'reasonable time' for the landlord to make the repair, absent evidence to the contrary?
choice_a: 7 days
choice_b: 3 days
choice_c: 14 days
choice_d: 30 days
explanation: Property Code Section 92.056 establishes a rebuttable presumption that seven days is a reasonable time for the landlord to repair after proper notice, though courts may consider the date notice was received, the severity of the condition, and the availability of materials and labor in evaluating whether that presumption should be overcome.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.056 (reasonable time to repair -- 7-day presumption), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.0561, a residential tenant who properly exercises the 'repair and deduct' remedy after the landlord fails to repair may deduct repair costs from rent up to:
choice_a: The greater of one month's rent or $500, with total deductions in a given month capped at that same amount
choice_b: An unlimited amount as long as receipts are provided
choice_c: A flat $100 regardless of the lease's monthly rent
choice_d: Half of one month's rent only
explanation: Property Code Section 92.0561 caps the repair-and-deduct remedy at the greater of one month's rent or $500 per repair, and further limits total repairs and deductions in any one month to that same combined cap -- while also requiring the tenant to use a licensed contractor and document the repair bill and payment.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.0561 (repair and deduct remedy -- dollar cap), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.056, a residential lease's provisions describing the tenant's repair remedies (such as repair-and-deduct or lease termination) must be presented in the lease:
choice_a: In underlined or conspicuous bold print
choice_b: In a separate document never attached to the lease
choice_c: Only orally at the time of signing
choice_d: In a font no larger than the rest of the lease, with no formatting requirement
explanation: Section 92.056 requires that a lease's description of the tenant's available repair remedies be set out in underlined or conspicuous bold print, mirroring the formatting requirement Chapter 92 imposes elsewhere (such as for advance-notice-of-surrender clauses affecting security deposits) to ensure tenants can readily see rights that limit or condition their remedies.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.056 (lease disclosure of repair remedies -- bold/underline requirement), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.331, a landlord's adverse action against a residential tenant (such as filing eviction or raising rent) taken within how many months after the tenant makes a good-faith repair complaint or joins a tenant organization is presumed retaliatory?
choice_a: 6 months
choice_b: 12 months
choice_c: 90 days
choice_d: 2 months
explanation: Property Code Section 92.331 prohibits landlord retaliation against a tenant who, in good faith, exercises a lease or statutory right (such as requesting repairs, reporting code violations, or organizing a tenant association), and creates a presumption of retaliation for covered landlord actions taken within six months of the tenant's protected conduct.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.331 (retaliation -- six-month presumption period), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.156, after a residential tenant moves out, the landlord must rekey any key-, card-, or combination-operated security device before the next tenant moves in, at:
choice_a: The landlord's own expense, within a reasonable time not later than the seventh day after the prior tenant surrenders the premises
choice_b: The new tenant's expense exclusively
choice_c: No particular deadline, so long as it happens eventually
choice_d: The prior tenant's expense, deducted automatically regardless of any lease provision
explanation: Property Code Section 92.156 requires the landlord to rekey security devices at the landlord's own expense within seven days after a tenant vacates, though a tenant may separately request additional rekeying at the tenant's own expense, and the landlord may only deduct rekeying costs from a departing tenant's deposit if the lease contains an underlined or bold-print provision authorizing it.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.156 (rekeying security devices between tenants), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.008, if a residential landlord unlawfully interrupts a tenant's water, electric, or gas service (other than for bona fide repairs, construction, or an emergency), the tenant's available remedies can include:
choice_a: Recovering possession, terminating the lease, and recovering actual damages plus one month's rent and $1,000
choice_b: No remedy at all, since utility service is solely between the tenant and the utility company
choice_c: Only a claim against the Real Estate Recovery Trust Account
choice_d: Automatic criminal prosecution of the landlord with no civil remedy
explanation: Property Code Section 92.008 bars a landlord from interrupting utilities furnished to a tenant except for bona fide repairs, construction, or an emergency, and gives a wrongfully affected tenant remedies including recovery of possession, lease termination, and damages of one month's rent plus $1,000, actual damages, and attorney's fees -- with any lease waiver of these protections void.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.008 (interruption of utilities -- tenant remedies), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.016, a residential tenant who is a victim of family violence and provides the landlord with a qualifying protective order or documentation from a health care or victim's advocate may terminate the lease early by:
choice_a: Providing the qualifying documentation and giving written notice of termination at least 30 days before vacating
choice_b: Simply vacating the unit with no notice of any kind
choice_c: Waiting until the lease naturally expires, since early termination is never available
choice_d: Obtaining written pre-approval from the landlord's attorney
explanation: Property Code Section 92.016 allows a tenant experiencing family violence to terminate the lease without continuing liability for future rent by providing the landlord a copy of qualifying documentation (such as a protective order or a statement from a health care provider or family violence advocate) and generally giving written notice at least 30 days before vacating; this right cannot be waived by the tenant, and leases must include statutory notice of it.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.016 (family violence -- early lease termination), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.201, when a residential tenant makes a written request for the name and address of the property's record title holder, the landlord must generally provide that disclosure within:
choice_a: 7 days of the request
choice_b: 48 hours of the request
choice_c: 30 days of the request
choice_d: There is no deadline; disclosure is entirely discretionary
explanation: Property Code Section 92.201 requires a landlord to disclose the name and address of the record title holder (and, if applicable, an off-site management company) to a requesting tenant, typically within seven days of the request, through written notice, continuous conspicuous posting, or inclusion in the lease or written rules.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.201 (disclosure of ownership and management), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.255, a landlord installing smoke alarms in a residential dwelling with multiple bedrooms opening onto the same interior hallway must, at minimum, install:
choice_a: A smoke alarm in the corridor or hallway in the immediate vicinity of the bedrooms, in addition to any other required alarms based on the unit's configuration
choice_b: No smoke alarm at all if the unit has fewer than three bedrooms
choice_c: Exactly one smoke alarm for the entire dwelling regardless of its size or layout
choice_d: A smoke alarm only in the kitchen
explanation: Property Code Section 92.255 sets specific smoke alarm placement rules depending on a unit's configuration -- including a corridor-area alarm serving bedrooms that share a hallway, an in-room alarm for single-room units, and at least one alarm on each level of a multi-level dwelling -- reflecting a more detailed statutory standard than a single blanket requirement.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.255 (smoke alarm placement requirements), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 92.259, if a residential tenant gives written notice requesting the landlord install, inspect, or repair a required smoke alarm, the landlord is liable for failing to act by:
choice_a: The seventh day after receiving the tenant's notice
choice_b: The first day after receiving the tenant's notice
choice_c: The 30th day after receiving the tenant's notice
choice_d: There is no deadline once the smoke alarm was properly installed at move-in
explanation: Property Code Section 92.259 makes a landlord liable both for failing to install a required smoke alarm at the time of initial occupancy and for failing to install, inspect, or repair a smoke alarm by the seventh day after receiving the tenant's written request, subject to specific statutory defenses available to the landlord under Section 92.261.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 92.259 (landlord's failure to install, inspect, or repair a smoke alarm), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Texas Property Code Chapter 91 (General Provisions Applicable to Landlords and Tenants) differs from Chapter 92 in that Chapter 91:
choice_a: Applies broadly to both residential and commercial tenancies, including default notice periods for terminating month-to-month tenancies, rather than being limited to residential leases
choice_b: Applies only to agricultural leases
choice_c: Was repealed and replaced entirely by Chapter 92
choice_d: Applies exclusively to manufactured home lot leases
explanation: Chapter 91 sets out general landlord-tenant provisions -- including, under Section 91.001, the default rule that a month-to-month tenancy of a month or more may be terminated by either party giving notice, with the tenancy ending one month after notice or on the date stated in the notice, whichever is later -- and these general provisions apply across both residential and commercial tenancies, unlike the residential-specific protections in Chapter 92.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 91.001 (general notice to terminate a periodic tenancy), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Chapter 93, which governs the landlord-tenant relationship for commercial rental property, 'commercial rental property' is defined as:
choice_a: Rental property that is not covered by Chapter 92's residential tenancy provisions
choice_b: Any property with more than four rental units regardless of use
choice_c: Only property zoned for retail use
choice_d: Property leased exclusively to a licensed real estate broker
explanation: Property Code Section 93.001 applies Chapter 93 to the landlord-tenant relationship for commercial rental property, which it defines simply as rental property that is not covered by Chapter 92 -- meaning Chapter 93, not Chapter 92, supplies the default statutory framework (including security deposit rules) for non-residential leases.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 93.001 (applicability of Chapter 93 -- commercial rental property), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 93.005, a commercial landlord must refund a tenant's security deposit within how many days after the tenant surrenders the premises, in contrast to the shorter deadline that applies to residential leases under Chapter 92?
choice_a: 60 days
choice_b: 30 days
choice_c: 10 days
choice_d: 15 days
explanation: Property Code Section 93.005 gives commercial landlords 60 days after the tenant surrenders the premises to refund the security deposit -- double the 30-day deadline Section 92.103 imposes on residential landlords -- while similarly providing that the tenant's claim to the deposit takes priority over the landlord's creditors, including a bankruptcy trustee.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 93.005 (commercial security deposit refund -- 60-day deadline), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under the Texas Manufactured Housing Standards Act (Occupations Code Chapter 1201), a 'HUD-code manufactured home' is generally distinguished from a 'mobile home' based on:
choice_a: Whether the structure was built after June 15, 1976, in compliance with federal manufactured housing construction and safety standards
choice_b: Whether the structure is currently occupied or vacant
choice_c: Whether the structure is single-wide or double-wide
choice_d: Whether the current owner financed the purchase with a chattel loan versus a real estate mortgage
explanation: Occupations Code Section 1201.003 defines a HUD-code manufactured home as a structure built after June 15, 1976, in accordance with the federal manufactured home construction and safety standards, on a permanent chassis and designed for use as a dwelling; a structure meeting similar physical specifications but built before that date is instead classified as a 'mobile home.'
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Sec. 1201.003 (HUD-code manufactured home vs. mobile home -- June 15, 1976 cutoff), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Occupations Code Section 1201.101, a person must hold a manufactured home retailer's license before:
choice_a: Selling or exchanging, or offering to sell or exchange, two or more manufactured homes to consumers in this state within a 12-month period
choice_b: Selling even a single manufactured home under any circumstances
choice_c: Repairing an appliance inside a manufactured home
choice_d: Renting out a manufactured home lot in a licensed community
explanation: Occupations Code Section 1201.101 requires a retailer's license for a person who sells or exchanges, or offers to sell or exchange, two or more manufactured homes to consumers in Texas within a 12-month period -- a volume-based licensing threshold distinct from the separate manufacturer's, broker's, installer's, and salesperson's license categories the same section establishes.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Sec. 1201.101 (retailer's license requirement -- two-or-more-homes threshold), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Occupations Code Section 1201.101, a person who negotiates for others a contract for the sale or exchange of two or more manufactured homes to consumers, without taking title, must hold a:
choice_a: Broker's license
choice_b: Salesperson's license only, with no sponsoring retailer required
choice_c: Real estate broker's license issued by TREC
choice_d: No license is required for this activity
explanation: Occupations Code Section 1201.101 requires a broker's license for a person who negotiates for others a bargain or contract for the sale or exchange of two or more manufactured homes to consumers -- a distinct license category from the retailer's license (which covers a person selling homes on their own account) and separate from TREC's real estate broker licensing framework, since manufactured homes are regulated as a distinct product line under Chapter 1201.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Sec. 1201.101 (broker's license -- negotiating manufactured home sales for others), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Occupations Code Section 1201.2055, a manufactured home owner may elect to treat the home as real property only if the home is attached to:
choice_a: Real property owned by the home's owner, or land the owner holds under a qualifying long-term lease
choice_b: Any land whatsoever, regardless of who owns it or under what arrangement
choice_c: A recreational vehicle park space only
choice_d: Property already zoned exclusively for site-built homes
explanation: Occupations Code Section 1201.2055 conditions the real-property election on the manufactured home being attached to real property owned by the home's owner, or to land held under a long-term lease meeting department rules -- reflecting that a manufactured home otherwise remains personal property (chattel) under Texas law until this election is properly made and perfected.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Sec. 1201.2055 (real property election -- attachment requirement), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Occupations Code Section 1201.2055, once a manufactured home owner receives a statement of ownership reflecting an election to treat the home as real property, the owner must file a copy of that statement in the county's real property records and notify the department and the county's chief appraiser within:
choice_a: 60 days
choice_b: 10 days
choice_c: 1 year
choice_d: There is no filing deadline once the statement is issued
explanation: Occupations Code Section 1201.2055 requires the owner to file the statement of ownership copy in the real property records of the county where the home is located, and to notify both the department and the county chief appraiser, within 60 days of receiving the statement -- the election is only 'perfected' as real property once this filing and notification actually occurs.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Sec. 1201.2055 (real property election -- 60-day filing and notification deadline), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under the Texas Manufactured Housing Standards Act (Occupations Code Chapter 1201), the document the department issues that functions much like a certificate of title for a manufactured home, and that a purchaser generally needs to establish ownership, is called the:
choice_a: Statement of ownership
choice_b: General warranty deed
choice_c: Certificate of occupancy
choice_d: Abstract of title
explanation: The statement of ownership, issued by the department (and its predecessor documents, the document of title and certificate of attachment, which are treated as equivalent), serves as the manufactured home's title-equivalent record, documenting ownership, liens, and -- where applicable -- the owner's election to treat the home as real property.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Sec. 1201.201 (statement of ownership as title-equivalent document), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Occupations Code Section 1201.051, primary responsibility for administering and enforcing the Manufactured Housing Standards Act (Chapter 1201), including licensing of manufacturers, retailers, brokers, and installers, rests with:
choice_a: The director of the manufactured housing division (within the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs)
choice_b: The Texas Real Estate Commission (TREC) exclusively
choice_c: Each individual county's building inspector, with no state-level oversight
choice_d: The Texas Department of Motor Vehicles
explanation: Occupations Code Section 1201.051 directs the director to administer and enforce Chapter 1201, which governs the licensing of manufacturers, retailers, brokers, salespersons, and installers of manufactured housing in Texas -- an entirely separate regulatory and licensing structure from TREC's oversight of real estate brokers and salespersons.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Sec. 1201.051 (director's administration and enforcement authority), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: The Texas Property Code chapter governing the sale of timeshare interests, which is officially cited as the 'Texas Timeshare Act,' is:
choice_a: Chapter 221
choice_b: Chapter 92
choice_c: Chapter 5
choice_d: Chapter 41
explanation: Property Code Section 221.001 provides that Chapter 221 'shall be known and may be cited as the Texas Timeshare Act,' establishing the statutory framework governing timeshare plan disclosures, purchaser cancellation rights, and related consumer protections distinct from ordinary residential real estate sales.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 221.001 (Texas Timeshare Act -- short title), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under the Texas Timeshare Act (Property Code Chapter 221), a 'timeshare interest' that gives the purchaser an actual estate interest in the underlying real property is called a timeshare:
choice_a: Estate, as distinguished from a timeshare use, which grants only a right to use accommodations without conveying any real property interest
choice_b: License, which is legally identical to a timeshare use
choice_c: Deed, a term the statute does not actually define
choice_d: Fee simple, regardless of whether real property rights are conveyed
explanation: Property Code Section 221.002 defines 'timeshare interest' as either a timeshare estate or a timeshare use: a timeshare estate conveys an actual interest in the underlying real property along with the right to use accommodations for a set period, while a timeshare use grants only a contractual right to use accommodations without any conveyed real property interest -- an important distinction for how each is treated under Texas property law.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 221.002 (timeshare estate vs. timeshare use), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 221.041, a timeshare purchaser generally has the right to cancel the purchase contract before the sixth day after whichever of the following occurs later:
choice_a: The date the purchaser signs and receives a copy of the purchase contract, or the date the purchaser receives the required timeshare disclosure statement
choice_b: The date the developer records the timeshare plan with the county
choice_c: The date construction of the timeshare property is completed
choice_d: There is no cancellation right once the contract is signed
explanation: Property Code Section 221.041 gives a timeshare purchaser roughly a six-day cancellation window, running from whichever occurs later of: (1) signing and receiving a copy of the purchase contract, or (2) receiving the mandatory timeshare disclosure statement -- and this right cannot be waived, with any purported waiver being voidable by the purchaser.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 221.041 (purchaser's right to cancel -- six-day period), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under the Texas Timeshare Act, a purchase contract provision purporting to waive the purchaser's statutory right to cancel the timeshare purchase within the cancellation period is:
choice_a: Voidable by the purchaser, since the cancellation right cannot be waived
choice_b: Fully enforceable if the purchaser initials the waiver clause
choice_c: Automatically void as to the entire contract, cancelling the purchase outright
choice_d: Enforceable only if reviewed by an attorney at closing
explanation: Property Code Section 221.041(b) specifically provides that a purchase contract provision waiving the purchaser's cancellation right is voidable by the purchaser -- meaning the purchaser can disregard the waiver clause and still exercise the statutory right to cancel, rather than the waiver invalidating the entire agreement outright.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 221.041(b) (non-waivable cancellation right), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under the Texas Timeshare Act's disclosure requirements, any deposit a purchaser makes in connection with buying a timeshare interest must be:
choice_a: Held by an escrow agent until the purchaser's right to cancel the contract has expired, and returned to the purchaser if the contract is timely cancelled
choice_b: Immediately released to the developer upon signing, with no escrow requirement
choice_c: Forfeited automatically if the purchaser later attempts to cancel
choice_d: Deposited directly with the Texas Real Estate Commission
explanation: Property Code Section 221.032's required disclosures inform purchasers that any deposit connected to a timeshare purchase must be held by an escrow agent until the cancellation period expires, with the funds returned to the purchaser if the purchaser exercises the statutory right to cancel -- protecting buyers during the mandatory rescission window.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 221.032 (timeshare deposit escrow requirement pending cancellation period), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Government Code Section 2306.581, a 'colonia' is generally defined as a geographic area located in a county within how many miles of the international border, containing 11 or more closely clustered dwellings in a community or neighborhood setting, with a majority low-income population?
choice_a: 150 miles
choice_b: 500 miles
choice_c: 25 miles
choice_d: 10 miles
explanation: Government Code Section 2306.581 defines a colonia as a geographic area in a county some part of which lies within 150 miles of the international border, containing 11 or more dwellings located close together in a community or neighborhood, with a majority population of low-income and very-low-income individuals and families (or, alternatively, an area determined by the department to have the physical and economic characteristics of a colonia) -- these substandard, often unplatted border-area subdivisions are the target of Texas's colonias-related statutes.
source_note: Texas Government Code Sec. 2306.581 (definition of 'colonia'), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Water Code Section 16.341, an 'affected county' subject to special colonia-related water and sewer service statutes includes a county whose average per capita income and unemployment rate, over three consecutive years, are:
choice_a: At least 25% below and 25% above the statewide averages, respectively, or a county adjacent to or within 100 miles of the international border meeting other statutory criteria
choice_b: Exactly equal to the statewide averages
choice_c: Irrelevant, since 'affected county' status depends solely on population size
choice_d: At least 50% above the statewide average income with no unemployment criterion
explanation: Water Code Section 16.341 defines an 'affected county' using economic-distress criteria (per capita income averaging at least 25% below, and unemployment averaging at least 25% above, the statewide averages over three consecutive years) as well as geographic criteria tied to proximity to the international border -- these designations trigger specialized statutory tools (such as model subdivision rules) aimed at colonias and other underserved border-area developments.
source_note: Texas Water Code Sec. 16.341 (definition of 'affected county'), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Local Government Code Section 232.023, a subdivider platting a subdivision where at least one lot is five acres or less must attach to the plat a document, in both English and Spanish, describing the subdivision's water and sewer facilities, along with:
choice_a: A Texas-licensed engineer's certification that the proposed facilities comply with the applicable model rules, plus a certified cost estimate to install them
choice_b: A notarized promise from the subdivider alone, with no engineering review required
choice_c: Nothing further; the English/Spanish description alone satisfies the statute
choice_d: A federal EPA permit issued specifically for the subdivision
explanation: Local Government Code Section 232.023 requires a Texas-licensed engineer to certify that a subdivision's proposed water and sewer facilities comply with model rules adopted under Water Code Section 16.343, along with a certified cost estimate for installing those facilities -- part of Texas's statutory response to unregulated, substandard colonia-style subdivisions that historically lacked basic water and sewer infrastructure along the border.
source_note: Texas Local Government Code Sec. 232.023 (plat requirements -- engineer certification of water/sewer facilities), verified via statutes.capitol.texas.gov / texas.public.law
